summary: Specifies how elliptic curve public keys are written in the Subject Public Key Information field of certificates. It describes the syntax and meaning of this field and updates parts of the earlier X.509 algorithm specification. This lets certificates carry keys for elliptic curve cryptography in a standard way.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5480 defines how X.509 certificates identify elliptic-curve public keys and encode their curve parameters. It also sets rules for key formats and for the uses a certificate may permit.

how are elliptic curve keys encoded in certificates
subtitle: How elliptic-curve public keys and their named curves are encoded in X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: Certificates need a consistent way to identify an elliptic-curve public key, its algorithm, and the curve parameters needed to interpret it.
tldr.mechanism: The SubjectPublicKeyInfo field contains an algorithm identifier with named-curve parameters and a public key encoded as an ECPoint in a BIT STRING.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5480 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3279 and is itself updated by RFC 8813.

today: RFC 5480 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3279 and is itself updated by RFC 8813.

sections.title: The Certificate Field Being Defined
sections.content:
RFC 5480 specifies the subjectPublicKeyInfo field in X.509 certificates that use Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC). It covers public keys for the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH), and Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV).

The field identifies the public-key algorithm and carries the public key itself. The RFC updates Sections 2.3.5 and 5, and the ASN.1 module, of RFC 3279 so that certificate authorities and relying parties can use a consistent definition.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate field names the kind of elliptic-curve key and contains the key itself. This RFC gives certificate creators and readers the same encoding rules.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Named Curves
sections.content:
The algorithm part of SubjectPublicKeyInfo contains an algorithm identifier and its parameters. id-ecPublicKey is unrestricted except for limits in the certificate's key-usage extension and must be supported. id-ecDH and id-ecMQV restrict the key to their respective key-agreement algorithms and may be supported.

All three identifiers require ECParameters. The only permitted choice is namedCurve, which identifies the curve by object identifier. implicitCurve and specifiedCurve must not be used, and a certificate without curve parameters must be rejected. The RFC lists identifiers for fifteen NIST-recommended curves.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate must name the curve that defines the public key. It must also identify whether the key is unrestricted or limited to a named key-agreement algorithm.

sections.title: Encoding the Public Key
sections.content:
The public key is an ECPoint, represented as an OCTET STRING and mapped bit for bit into the certificate's BIT STRING. Implementations must support the uncompressed form; they may support the compressed form. The hybrid form must not be used.

The first octet identifies the form. 0x04 indicates an uncompressed point, while 0x02 or 0x03 indicates a compressed point. A public key with any other first octet must be rejected.
sections.plainLanguage: The key bytes start with a code that identifies their format. Readers must accept uncompressed keys and reject a key that starts with an unassigned format code.

sections.title: Key-Usage Rules
sections.content:
A certificate's keyUsage extension states the permitted uses of its key. With id-ecPublicKey, a CA certificate may combine digital-signature, key-agreement, certificate-signing, and revocation-list-signing uses as specified in the RFC. For an end-entity certificate, the permitted choices are digital signature, non-repudiation, and key agreement.

With id-ecDH or id-ecMQV, a present key-usage extension must include keyAgreement. It may include encipherOnly or decipherOnly, but must not include digital-signature, non-repudiation, key-transport, certificate-signing, or revocation-list-signing uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The key-usage extension limits what a certificate's key can do. Keys identified only for ECDH or ECMQV are for key agreement, not signing or certificate issuance.

sections.title: Choosing Curves and Hashes
sections.content:
A certificate authority choosing an ECDSA signature needs to consider the public-key size, hash algorithm, and curve together. The RFC recommends that their security strengths be roughly equivalent and gives recommended combinations, including secp256r1 with SHA-256 and secp384r1 with SHA-384.

The RFC warns that curves without broad review may have weaknesses and requires validation of candidate public keys against their domain parameters. It also notes that using a larger hash and then truncating it costs processing, especially on constrained devices. MD2 and MD5 are discouraged for new applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a curve, key size, and hash with comparable security strength. Validate the public key against the named curve's parameters before relying on it.

sections.title: ASN.1 Module and Registrations
sections.content:
Appendix A provides an ASN.1 module containing the ECC definitions and the relevant non-ECC definitions from RFC 3279. It is a conformant subset of the X9.62 module. An implementation that needs the additional X9.62 options should use that module; the RFC notes that the modules may produce different PER encodings.

The document uses object identifiers for public-key types, curves, algorithms, and its ASN.1 module. It states that no further action by IANA is necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix provides one ASN.1 module for these certificate definitions. The RFC makes no new request for IANA action.
